note: Number columns are accounting conventions, never people: no commentator produced a number for this population. The authors section is text: what each argues, what the claim is about, the convention in this ledger that comes closest (if any) and why it is not the same thing. External links live in sources.json, keyed to the ids used here. The preset marked central is the page's reference case, the adopted main case (main_case_2026_10_07). A preset with extends starts from that preset's settings and changes only its own. A setting reads a number through value_from (a name, or a list of names for a band): a plain name is a field of derived/scaling_check.json, and responses.<path> reads the case payload's meta.responses. A setting's cite lists ids in sources.json; the build refuses an id the registry lacks or one that does not name the convention among its places. In any string, {response:<id>} becomes that meta.responses entry's low and high responses, {share:<id>} its population share, {elasticity:<id>} the marginal rates it is read from, {people:<field>} a count of meta.lineage.counts in millions and {rate:<name>} a rate of meta.capital_return, so no number of the case is typed by hand; {assigned:<name>} is filled from the ledger when the page draws. lane_readings are states the case lane ran, each the central preset with stated changes, checked by test_engine.js against the lane's file; readouts are figures of the case read from a lane file, which the page shows beside the presets because it cannot compute them.

presets.label: Main case
presets.summary: The case adopted on 2026-10-07. It counts the {people:account_union} people the survey identifies and the {people:added} descendants who no longer report Mexican origin, as whole people. Schools are charged at their full average cost per pupil, colleges and the other services in full, roads and parks at their long-run response, and general government at {response:general_government} of average cost. The Social Security and Medicare Part A benefits the group earns as it works count as they are earned, at what current law can pay, and retiree health the same way. Public capital earns a real return of {rate:low} to {rate:high}, and every government enterprise responds. Police, courts and prisons are charged by use, free hospital care by uninsured use, and rental assistance as a benefit. Defense, interest on existing debt and business subsidies are held fixed. The gain from the group's work is counted.
presets.scope_note: The case and its readings come from main_case_2026_10_07/RESULT.md and decisions/2026-10-07-main-case-v6.md; the INDEX's table of cases lists the adoptions it builds on. The long-run evidence is read twice. At the low reading general government takes the low end of its band, roads and parks their low responses and capital {rate:low}; at the high reading each takes its high end and capital {rate:high}. Both readings enter the range with the account's other open choices. The capital return is an imputed resource cost and never a debt flow. Holding defense and interest at zero is the account's assumption.

settings.label: Social Security and Medicare Part A
settings.note: Counted as the group earns them: the promises its payroll taxes buy, at the benefits current law can pay, on the 2026 Trustees Reports and current law's separate OASI and DI funds. Counted when paid instead, this is the cash set.

settings.label: School spending
settings.note: Charged at the full average cost per pupil: a school system sized for the group's pupils. Across districts and across states, school spending scales about one for one with enrollment. CBO's year-to-year rates, the grey ticks, give only the first year's budget response.

settings.label: College and other education
settings.note: Grows with enrollment in full. At 0, college budgets are held fixed too, the case's other benchmark.

settings.label: Roads, transport and parks
settings.note: At their long-run response: how spending on each road, transport and park function scales with population across the states, read over a removal of the group's size, {response:economic_affairs_services} for roads and economic affairs and {response:recreation_culture} for parks. Roads are keyed by vehicle miles and freight.

settings.label: General government
settings.note: Tax collection, financial management and state and local administration grow as they do across the states, at marginal rates of {elasticity:general_government}. The group is {share:general_government} of residents, and when cost is a power of population, removing a share that large saves more than the marginal rate: {response:general_government} of average cost.

settings.label: General government, both values
settings.note: Both values enter the range, each with its reading of the long-run evidence.

settings.label: Police, courts, prisons
settings.note: Charged by use instead of per head: prisons by custody, police half by arrests and half per head, the criminal part of the courts by arrests, border enforcement per head. The national total is unchanged; only the group's part of it moves.

settings.label: Medicaid, CHIP and other medical
settings.note: Governments repay part of hospitals' free care for the uninsured. The account's keys are built from measured payments, which record no free care, so the part they under-charge is keyed to the group's share of uninsured person-years at equal use.

settings.label: Medicaid, CHIP and other medical, both ends
settings.note: Both ends of the lane's range enter the range of open choices.

settings.label: Return on public capital
settings.note: A real return of {rate:low} at the low reading and {rate:high} at the high one on the public capital the group's services and enterprises use: what the money tied up in schools, roads and utilities would cost to borrow. Budgets charge depreciation and no return, so without it public capital is priced below its cost. The {rate:reported} return to private capital prices the capital displaced from private use, a social cost rather than a budget cost.

settings.label: Government enterprises
settings.note: Every government enterprise responds: transit, public housing, water, sewers, power, airports, ports and tolls run at a loss, and the group is charged its share of that loss and of the return on their capital.

settings.label: Reading of the long-run evidence
settings.note: The single result in the bar takes the low reading.

settings.label: Readings of the long-run evidence, both
settings.note: Both enter the range of open choices.

misses: Costs outside government budgets: crime victims' harm, delay on roads, the free hospital care that hospitals and private payers absorb, and the rent other renters pay to landlords who are also residents. research/immigration-real-fiscal-and-social-costs-2026-09-23.md prices them beside the account; none is added to it.
What a removal would save in its first year: the first-year budget response, beside the presets.
Interest on the debt past deficits left behind and the unfunded legacy of public pensions: both are stated beside the account.
The welfare of the group's own members and of Mexico's residents: world_ledger_2026_09_27/RESULT.md sets the case against the group living in Mexico.
Gains from ideas, specialization and fixed costs: the production model has constant returns (see "Objections, with the result this repo computed for each").

standing.title: Whose ledger is this?
rows: This page. The taxes the group pays, the benefits and services it draws, the public capital it uses, and the gain from its work that reaches everyone else.
What they earn here against what they would earn in Mexico, known as the place premium. It is inside US GDP but not in this ledger, and it is where most of any world-GDP gain sits.
In the world ledger, beside this page
Effects on Mexico: money sent home, workers departed, its budget without them.
In the world ledger, in part
standing.text: Claims about world GDP add all three. They cannot be netted against this page's number without deciding how much a dollar to a migrant counts against a dollar to someone already here, which is a moral weight, not a measurement. The world ledger (world_ledger_2026_09_27/RESULT.md) sets the main case against the group living in Mexico and states the weight at which the sum changes sign. Interest on US debt would never be deducted from world GDP: it is a payment from taxpayers to bondholders, a transfer, and no output is lost. Inside this ledger it is held fixed because debt already issued does not shrink when a population is smaller.

authors.name: Noah Smith
argues: He cites CBO's July 2024 projection: the 2021-26 surge lowers covered federal deficits by about $0.9tn over 2024-2034. CBO's headline excludes discretionary appropriations and state and local budgets.

In his own words the same arrivals are "a long-term fiscal problem, because these people will require heavy government support for their health care, housing, and education; this will end up coming from city and state governments".
authors.object: A recent surge of all origins, the federal budget, a ten-year window.

closest.why: A claim about the federal budget does not charge schools or police, which are almost entirely state and local. He names that local cost himself and does not net it against the federal gain. The repo's September revision no longer calls this a contradiction.

leaves_out: The second generation: 'no mention of the second generation' (scorecard :35). Most of this population is US-born.
A number for the gain from production or complementary skills: none is recorded.

authors.name: Matthew Yglesias
argues: He states no fiscal number in his own voice. The CBO material on Slow Boring is in guest posts (Kolko, 2024-09-12; Elmendorf and Williams, 2023-08-28).

His case is scale and growth, lower grocery and service prices, and hours freed for high-wage women. On cost he has one aside, in a sentence about housing: the tools to end housing shortages, "like immigration", "would cost taxpayers nothing". He concedes congestion costs (traffic, rent, water, pollution) and that crime counts rise with population.
authors.object: Immigrants 'of virtually all stripes', national scale, no stated horizon.

closest.why: This is the condition under which immigration "would cost taxpayers nothing" holds in this ledger. That is an inference from his aside; he did not argue it. His price channel is outside the account (see the objections section).

leaves_out: Local budgets: 'He addresses wages, not local budgets' (audit :67).
The National Academies 2016 report, and any federal, Social Security or debt number of his own (audit :138-139).

authors.name: Bryan Caplan
argues: A moral presumption in favor of free migration, and an economic case that is 'extremely strong': very large global gains from moving labor to productive places. The 'double world GDP' figure is sourced to openborders.info, not to a sentence of his.
Restrictions 'are not necessary to protect American taxpayers': fiscal effects are modest, and where they are not, cheaper keyhole remedies exist (entry fees, surtaxes, exclusion from benefits).
authors.object: Future entrants under open borders; the welfare of migrants and the world as well as natives.

closest.why: No setting of this ledger represents his claim, so no number is shown. His large gains accrue mainly to the migrants themselves (the second row of the table above), and his keyhole remedy applies to future entrants: it cannot be applied to a resident population that is mostly US-born citizens. Switching benefits off in this ledger would only stop counting {assigned:benefits} bn of costs; it would not be his argument.

leaves_out: School, shelter and service load on state and local budgets: what survives an exclusion from welfare (audit :288). The audit's verdict on the taxpayer claim: 'Federal gains can coexist with state/local costs in education, shelter, and related services'.
The cost and feasibility of the keyhole instruments themselves (audit :216).

authors.name: Nicholas Decker
argues: 'Immigrants must make us richer': "I think the assumption of constant returns to scale is nonsense. Not only that, it is obvious nonsense… There are three main channels by which returns simply have to be increasing: specialization, ideas, and fixed costs… of course immigrants make us richer."
authors.object: All immigrants; the total income of people already here; no horizon or cost convention stated.

closest.why: His argument has a production side and no fiscal side. But this ledger's production model has constant returns, the assumption he rejects, so its near-zero private gain is this account's result and not a test of his claim. The repo has withdrawn two of its own earlier rebuttals of him.

leaves_out: Every fiscal line: the audits record him compressing the question into 'one production-function dispute' (audit 2026-04-11 :255-256).
Composition: his July 2026 proposal to rank visas concedes that composition decides the sign (scorecard :79).
